q1303: "He will rejoice over thee with joy, he will rest in his love, he will joy over thee with singing" (Zephaniah 3:17). The Bible shows a God who delights in His children personally. Jesus stopped busy adults and welcomed little children, took them in His arms and blessed them (Mark 10:13-16). Psalm 127:3 calls children a heritage from the LORD, and Psalm 149:4 says the LORD takes pleasure in His people. God's attention is not divided or rushed. He knows each person by name. Special time, ten or fifteen minutes of undivided, child-led attention, is a small earthly picture of that delight. It tells a child, in a way they can feel, that they are wanted and enjoyed.
q1304: Children have a deep need for attention and connection. When they do not get enough positive attention, many will seek it in other ways, including misbehaviour, because the brain values connection highly. Predictable one-to-one time meets that need ahead of time. When a parent follows the child's lead, describing and praising without correcting, the child feels competent and seen. This can release feel-good chemicals linked with bonding and reduce stress. Studies of programmes that use child-led play suggest it can reduce defiance and strengthen the parent-child relationship. Because special time happens at the same time each day, the child's brain learns to expect it, which lowers anxiety. Over weeks the relationship often warms and cooperation grows.
q1305: God designed children to grow best inside relationships where they feel delighted in, not merely managed. Love that only shows up to correct or instruct feels thin. Love that also plays, listens and enjoys builds a deep sense of worth. This reflects God's character. He is not only a Lord who commands but a Father who rejoices over His children. When parents give special time, they show that a child's presence is a joy in itself, not something earned. That experience forms a child's sense of identity and prepares them to believe that God delights in them too. It also refreshes parents, reminding them of the gift their children are, and healing the strain of busy family life.
q1306: "Rejoice with them that do rejoice, and weep with them that weep" (Romans 12:15). The Bible takes emotions seriously. The Psalms are full of joy, grief, fear and anger poured out to God, and Psalm 62:8 invites us to pour out our hearts before Him. "Jesus wept" (John 11:35), showing that even the Son of God felt deep sorrow. Ephesians 4:26 shows that anger can be felt without sinning. God listens to every feeling and then guides what we do with it. Emotion coaching follows this pattern. Parents notice and accept their child's feelings, help name them, and then set limits on behaviour and solve problems together, just as God does with us.
q1307: When a feeling is noticed and named, the emotional and thinking parts of the brain begin to work together. Research suggests that putting a feeling into words can calm the brain's alarm centre. Catching feelings while they are still small makes this easier, because the stress response has not fully taken over. Listening and saying "That makes sense" lowers defensiveness and helps the child feel safe. Over time, children learn a vocabulary for emotions, which gives them more control. Studies of families who coach emotions have found children with better self-control, stronger friendships and better school results. As this is practised over weeks, the brain pathways linking feeling, words and wise action grow stronger.
q1308: God designed emotions as messengers, signals that something matters. Fear warns of danger, sadness marks loss, anger signals something is wrong, and joy celebrates good. They are part of being made in His image, since God Himself is described as rejoicing, grieving and being angry at injustice. The aim is not to crush feelings but to understand and steer them. Emotion coaching teaches children that their feelings are welcome but their actions still matter. This mirrors God's grace and truth together. Children who learn this can bring their feelings honestly to God in prayer rather than hiding them. Over time, this leads to emotional maturity, compassion for others and a faith that is real in every season.
q1309: "And be ye kind one to another, tenderhearted, forgiving one another, even as God for Christ's sake hath forgiven you" (Ephesians 4:32). The Bible gives a clear pattern for repair. Matthew 5:23-24 tells us to leave our gift at the altar and first be reconciled. James 5:16 invites us to confess our faults one to another, and Colossians 3:13 calls us to forgive as Christ forgave us. God Himself is the great repairer. When we wrong Him, He makes the way back, through Christ. When a parent calms down, goes to their child, owns the wrong and reconnects, they are living out this gospel pattern in the most ordinary moments of family life.
q1310: When a parent yells or is unfair, a child's stress system is activated and they may feel fear, shame or confusion. Without repair, children often decide it was their fault. Repair helps undo this. Calming yourself first means your nervous system is settled enough to be gentle. Getting to their level and owning it simply, "I'm sorry I yelled," helps the child's brain understand what happened. Saying "You didn't deserve that" lifts shame. Reconnecting through a hug or a game helps restore feelings of safety. Research on early relationships suggests that frequent small ruptures followed by repair are normal and can build resilience. Over weeks and months, children learn that relationships can break and be mended.
q1311: God did not design relationships to be perfect, but to be repairable. Since we are all imperfect, the ability to mend after hurt is essential for love to last. Children who experience repair learn that mistakes do not end love, and they learn how to apologise and forgive themselves. This reflects the very heart of God. He does not abandon relationship when we fail. He comes to restore it, at great cost to Himself. When parents repair, they also model humility, showing that admitting wrong is a strength. This prepares children for friendships, marriages and church life, where repair is constantly needed. Through repair, families become places where grace is not just taught but lived.
q1312: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee: The LORD make his face shine upon thee, and be gracious unto thee: The LORD lift up his countenance upon thee, and give thee peace" (Numbers 6:24-26). God commanded the priests to speak this over His people regularly. Jacob laid hands on his grandsons and blessed them (Genesis 48:15-16), and Jesus took children in His arms, put His hands on them and blessed them (Mark 10:16). Proverbs 18:21 says death and life are in the power of the tongue. God blesses before He commands. Blessing is His first word over creation and over His people, and parents who bless their children share in that same life-giving speech.
q1313: Children absorb the words spoken over them repeatedly, and over time those words can become part of their inner voice. Research on child development suggests that warm, affirming words from parents are linked with healthier self-esteem and resilience. Gentle touch, such as a hand on the shoulder or head, can lower stress and support bonding. Speaking a blessing at a predictable time, like bedtime or a meal, makes it part of the rhythm of family life, and repeated positive experiences help strengthen the brain pathways linked with security. Adding one specific thing you love about your child makes it personal and real. Over weeks and months, these daily words shape how a child sees themselves and God.
q1314: God designed us to be shaped by words, especially the words of those we love. That is why He speaks blessing over His people and calls parents to do the same. A child who hears every day that they are loved, kept and given peace by God carries that truth into a world that often says the opposite. This reflects God's generous character. He gives His favour freely, before we earn anything. The family blessing becomes a channel for that grace, passing faith from one generation to the next in a simple, warm way. Over time it builds a child's identity on God's love rather than on performance, and it strengthens the bond between parent and child.
q1315: From the very first pages of Scripture, God gives people real choices inside loving limits. In Eden there were many trees to enjoy and one boundary to keep (Genesis 2:16-17). Through Moses, God set the options plainly before His people and urged them toward the good one, saying, "I have set before you life and death, blessing and cursing: therefore choose life" (Deuteronomy 30:19). Joshua did the same at Shechem (Joshua 24:15), and Paul reminds us that freedom is given to be used in love (Galatians 5:13). God does not drag us like mules. He invites, explains, and then lets our choice matter. When a parent fixes the non-negotiable and then offers two good options, or says "when your shoes are on, then we go," they are echoing the way the Father raises His own children.
q1316: A child's brain is still building the pathways that handle self-control and planning, which sit in the front of the brain and mature slowly through the teenage years. A flat command can feel to a young child like a threat to their small sense of control, and the stress system pushes back with protest or freezing. A choice between two acceptable options gives that need for control somewhere safe to go. The child pauses, weighs, decides, and in doing so exercises the very part of the brain that later handles bigger decisions. When-then statements add a clear pattern of cause and effect. Calm, repeated follow-through teaches the child that your words are reliable, so over weeks the battles usually shorten. Your own calm voice also helps steady their nervous system, because children borrow regulation from the adults near them.
q1317: God could have made us like machines that simply obey, but love cannot grow without real choice. He made children with a strong drive to say "I can do it myself" because He means them to grow into adults who choose good freely, not only under pressure. Limited choices honour both sides of His design. The boundary reflects His holiness and care, and the choice reflects His respect for the person He made. This is how the Father treats us, patient with our small steps, firm about what truly matters, and generous with freedom wherever it is safe. A parent who works this way is not losing authority. They are training a conscience and a will, so that one day the child can stand on their own and say, as Joshua did, that they choose to serve the Lord.
q1318: Scripture often shows God meeting His people not in noise but in quiet. Elijah, worn out and afraid, found that the Lord was not in the wind, the earthquake or the fire, but in "a still small voice" (1 Kings 19:12). The psalmist says, "Truly my soul waiteth upon God: from him cometh my salvation" (Psalm 62:1), and Isaiah records God's word that "in quietness and in confidence shall be your strength" (Isaiah 30:15). Psalm 46 places the command "Be still, and know that I am God" in the middle of roaring nations and shaking mountains. Stillness is not a technique to make God appear. He is already present. Silence is simply the act of stopping long enough to notice Him, laying down our talking and performing, and letting Him be God while we rest as His children.
q1319: Modern life keeps the brain flooded with input, and much of that input keeps the alarm system lightly switched on. When you put your phone in another room, sit with feet on the floor and let your shoulders drop, you remove many of those small triggers. Slow breathing tells the vagus nerve, a long nerve linking brain, heart and gut, that you are safe, and in studies heart rate and breathing tend to slow during silence. Reading one short verse gives the mind a gentle anchor. Each time you notice a wandering thought and return, you exercise attention, a little like lifting a light weight. Over days and weeks this practice seems to make it easier to settle, so the calm you meet in the chair begins to show up in traffic and in hard conversations too.
q1320: God made us as creatures who need rest, not just at night but in the middle of the day's demands. He built a Sabbath into the week and evenings into every day, and He designed our bodies with a calming branch of the nervous system that only switches on when we stop rushing. Stillness reflects His character because God is not anxious. He is never hurried, never scrambling, never afraid that things will fall apart. When we sit quietly before Him, we are invited into His own unhurried peace. It is also deeply relational. Friends who are truly close can sit together without words, and God offers us that kind of closeness. Ending with a simple "Thank You that You are here" turns a calming exercise into communion, and over time it heals the restless heart.
q1321: When Scripture speaks of meditation, it does not mean emptying the mind. The Hebrew word hagah, used in Psalm 1:2 and Joshua 1:8, carries the sense of murmuring or growling softly, like a lion over its prey. "But his delight is in the law of the LORD, and in his law doth he meditate day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The psalmist adds, "I will meditate in thy precepts, and have respect unto thy ways" (Psalm 119:15), and Paul tells believers to let the word of Christ dwell in them richly (Colossians 3:16). The pattern is slow repetition until truth moves from the page into the heart. God meets us here by speaking through His word personally, so that a verse read a hundred times can suddenly become His fresh voice to us today.
